paragraphs.text: Every society has had to solve the same problem: food arrives in a rush and is eaten slowly. Drying, salting, smoking and fermenting are all older than writing, and all of them work by making life difficult for microbes — removing the water they need, raising the salt, or letting harmless organisms take the space before harmful ones arrive. None of these methods was understood in the modern sense until the nineteenth century, which did not prevent them from being refined to a remarkable degree by people who had no idea why they worked. A cheese, a dried fish and a jar of pickles are each the result of centuries of experiment with no theory behind it, and each is still made much as it was.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Canning was the first method invented to order. A French government offered a prize for a way of keeping food for an army on the move, and a confectioner won it in 1810 by sealing food in glass and heating it. His explanation was wrong — he believed that air itself spoiled food — but the procedure was right, and it spread quickly to tin-plated iron, which did not break in a wagon. The industry that followed ran for fifty years on a method whose mechanism nobody could state. That is less unusual than it sounds: a great deal of useful engineering has run ahead of the science that explains it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Understanding arrived with microbiology. Once spoilage was shown to be caused by living organisms carried in the air and on surfaces, the temperatures and times used in canning could be calculated rather than guessed, and the calculation mattered: the organism that causes botulism forms spores that survive boiling, and killing them requires a temperature above the boiling point of water, which is reached by heating under pressure. Low-acid foods are processed on that basis, and the rule is one of the few in the kitchen where the reasoning is worth knowing exactly. Acid foods are safer, because the organism does not grow below a certain acidity, which is why fruit can be bottled at the temperature of boiling water and beans cannot.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Cold came later than heat and changed more. Ice had been cut from lakes and stored in insulated houses for centuries, but mechanical refrigeration made cold available where no ice formed, and the effect on what people ate was larger than any single food technology before it. Meat could travel from one continent to another, milk could be collected from farms a day away rather than an hour, and the seasons in a city shop became suggestions. It also concentrated the industry, since the equipment favoured those who could afford it. A dairy with a cooling plant could collect from farms that a dairy without one could not serve, and the second dairy did not last long.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Freezing is a different process from chilling and has its own history. Slow freezing produces large ice crystals that rupture cell walls, which is why the first frozen foods were disliked; the commercial method that solved it, developed in the 1920s after its inventor watched fish freeze almost instantly in Arctic air, froze food fast enough to keep the crystals small. The principle has not changed since, and most of the progress in the century that followed has been in packaging and in the unbroken chain of cold between factory and freezer.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Later methods have chased the same goal with less heat. Food can be preserved by removing oxygen from the pack, by adding pressure of thousands of atmospheres for a few minutes, or by treatment with ultraviolet light, and each of these leaves the flavour and the vitamins closer to the fresh product than boiling does. All of them are more expensive than heat, all of them work on some foods and not others, and none of them has displaced the tin, which remains the cheapest way yet found to make a meal last five years without electricity.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The modern argument is less about safety than about loss. A third of the food grown in the world is never eaten, and the share is highest where preservation is weakest: in hot countries without reliable cold, most of the loss happens between the field and the market. The technologies that would help there are not the newest ones but the oldest ones done properly — shade, drying, simple cold rooms and packaging that keeps insects out — which is unglamorous, cheap by the standards of the problem, and still not installed.
paragraphs.label: G
